result.markdown: --- course-unit: ch05-stochastic-differential-equations status: complete --- # Stochastic differential equations ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 2, Session 2. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd). ::: A jump process resolves every infection and recovery. A stochastic differential equation (SDE) instead describes continuous-valued fluctuations around a drift. This is useful when the population is large enough for a diffusion approximation to be reasonable, and when we want to connect stochastic simulation with the calculus and solvers used for ODEs. ## Learning goals You will: - derive the chemical Langevin approximation from SIR reaction propensities; - distinguish drift, diffusion columns, and independent Wiener processes; - solve a non-diagonal-noise SDE with the current StochasticDiffEq API; and - diagnose conservation and the possibility of negative populations. ## Model assumptions and classification The baseline is the closed, homogeneously mixing SIR population $(S,I,R)=(990,10,0)$ with $N=1000$, $c=10.0$, $\beta=0.05$, and $\gamma=0.25$. We retain the two transitions $S+I\to 2I$ and $I\to R$, but replace integer event counts by a diffusion. This is a **stochastic, continuous-time, continuous-state, population-level** model. “Continuous state” means the numerical approximation can produce real values, not that people are fractional. It is an approximation to the discrete-state CTMC from Chapter 4, and is most defensible when propensities are large and the process is away from absorbing boundaries. ## Equations Write the stoichiometric columns and propensities as $$ V = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0\\ 1 & -1\\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad a(X)= \begin{pmatrix} \kappa SI\\ \gamma I \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \kappa=\frac{\beta c}{N}. $$ Take an interval $\Delta t$ that is *mesoscopic*: long enough that each reaction fires many times, yet short enough that the propensities barely move over it. On such an interval a Poisson event count with mean $a_j\Delta t$ can be approximated by $$ \operatorname{Poisson}(a_j\Delta t)\approx a_j\Delta t+\sqrt{a_j}\,\Delta W_j, $$ where $\Delta W_j$ are independent Brownian increments with variance $\Delta t$. The two requirements on $\Delta t$ pull against each other, and the differential notation $dt$ used below is the formal limit of this mesoscopic construction rather than a literally infinitesimal step. The Validation section returns to what that tension costs. A **Wiener process** $W(t)$ is the continuous-time limit of a random walk: it starts at $W(0)=0$, its increments over disjoint intervals are independent, and $W(t+dt)-W(t)\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,dt)$. So $dW$ has mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$ — which shrinks more slowly than $dt$ itself, and is why the noise term survives the small-$dt$ limit instead of disappearing beside the drift. The approximation above is the normal approximation to a Poisson count, and the three facts it needs are short enough to restate here. 1. In @sec-jump-processes the waiting time to the next reaction-$j$ event was exponential with rate $a_j$. Counting those events rather than timing them, the number occurring in a window of width $\Delta t$, short enough that the propensities barely move, is $\operatorname{Poisson}(a_j\Delta t)$. 2. A Poisson variable has equal mean and variance, both $a_j\Delta t$ here. 3. A Poisson variable with a large enough mean is close to a normal one matching those two moments, which is the substitution made above. So @sec-jump-processes resolves every event individually; here we keep only the mean and the variance and let the individual events blur together. The approximation therefore improves as events become more frequent, and degrades when counts are small, which is exactly when a compartment is close to empty. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## Optional background The exponential waiting time, its memorylessness, and the Poisson count that follows from it are derived in @sec-probability-and-stochastic-processes. That unit is optional: the three facts above are all this chapter uses, and nothing below depends on having read it. ::: Substituting both reactions into the time-change equation gives the chemical Langevin equation $$ dX = V a(X)\,dt + V\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{a(X)})\,dW. $$ {#eq-chemical-langevin} Thus the drift $f(X)=Va(X)$ is $$ f(X)=(-a_1,\ a_1-a_2,\ a_2)^\mathsf{T}, $$ and the $3\times2$ diffusion matrix $G(X)$ has columns $$ G_{\cdot1}=(-\sqrt{a_1},\sqrt{a_1},0)^\mathsf{T},\qquad G_{\cdot2}=(0,-\sqrt{a_2},\sqrt{a_2})^\mathsf{T}. $$ Because each column of $V$ sums to zero, both the drift and every Brownian increment conserve $S+I+R$ algebraically. Numerical integration can still accumulate roundoff error. ## Julia implementation `SDEProblem` accepts an in-place drift `f!` and diffusion `g!`. A vector-valued state with a $3\times2$ diffusion requires `noise_rate_prototype=zeros(3, 2)`: two columns correspond to the two independent Wiener processes. `LambaEM()` is the StochasticDiffEq method for Euler--Maruyama with general (non-diagonal) noise in the installed 7.1.1 environment. The unusual spelling is part of the package API. ::: {#cell-code-ch05-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using CairoMakie using OrdinaryDiffEq using StochasticDiffEq using StableRNGs const N = 1000.0 const β = 0.05 const c = 10.0 const γ = 0.25 const κ = β * c / N const u₀ = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0] const tspan = (0.0, 40.0) const times = collect(0.0:0.1:40.0) function propensities(u, p) κ, γ = p S, I = max(u[1], 0.0), max(u[2], 0.0) return (κ * S * I, γ * I) end ``` ::: {#code-ch05-setup .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` propensities (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: The `max` operations make the code well-defined if an Euler step crosses a boundary. They do not repair the interpretation of a negative state; the boundary issue is discussed below. ::: {#cell-code-ch05-kernel .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function sir_drift!(du, u, p, t) infection, recovery = propensities(u, p) du[1] = -infection du[2] = infection - recovery du[3] = recovery return nothing end function sir_diffusion!(G, u, p, t) infection, recovery = propensities(u, p) infection_noise = sqrt(infection) recovery_noise = sqrt(recovery) G[1, 1] = -infection_noise G[2, 1] = infection_noise G[3, 1] = 0.0 G[1, 2] = 0.0 G[2, 2] = -recovery_noise G[3, 2] = recovery_noise return nothing end noise_shape = zeros(3, 2) sde_problem = SDEProblem( sir_drift!, sir_diffusion!, u₀, tspan, (κ, γ); noise_rate_prototype = noise_shape, ) sde_solution = solve( sde_problem, LambaEM(); dt = 0.02, adaptive = false, saveat = times, rng = StableRNG(20250711), ) sde_states = Array(sde_solution) ``` ::: {#code-ch05-kernel .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3×401 Matrix{Float64}: 990.0 989.411 989.623 … 169.795 169.918 170.275 10.0 9.86467 10.446 5.09896 5.24484 5.00951 0.0 0.723904 -0.0688276 825.106 824.837 824.715 ``` ::: ::: The function `sir_diffusion!` is a direct transcription of the two columns of $G$ in Equation @eq-chemical-langevin. It is intentionally not replaced by independent noise on $S$, $I$, and $R$: doing that would break the reaction-level correlation and population conservation. For a baseline comparison, solve the drift alone: ::: {#cell-code-ch05-ode .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} ode_problem = ODEProblem(sir_drift!, u₀, tspan, (κ, γ)) ode_solution = solve(ode_problem, Tsit5(); saveat = times) ode_states = Array(ode_solution) mass_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(sde_states; dims = 1)) .- N)) minimum_state = minimum(sde_states) @assert mass_error < 1e-8 (; mass_error, minimum_state) ``` ::: {#code-ch05-ode .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (mass_error = 2.7284841053187847e-12, minimum_state = -0.06882763332898889) ``` ::: ::: The ODE is not the expected trajectory of every SDE path, but it is the large-population drift comparison. The conservation assertion is stronger: it checks a structural property of the implementation independently of the random realization. ::: {#cell-fig-ch05-diffusion .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (760, 430)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "people", title = "Chemical Langevin SIR") for (j, (name, color)) in enumerate(zip(["S", "I", "R"], [:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen])) lines!(ax, times, sde_states[j, :]; color, linewidth = 2, label = "$name (SDE)") lines!(ax, times, ode_states[j, :]; color, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1.5, label = "$name (ODE)") end axislegend(ax, position = :rt, nbanks = 2) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch05-diffusion .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` A chemical-Langevin SIR path compared with the deterministic drift. ::: ::: ## Validation The noise columns sum to zero, so conservation is a useful first test. We can also check the diffusion construction directly at one valid state: ::: {#code-ch05-validation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} G = zeros(3, 2) sir_diffusion!(G, [900.0, 80.0, 20.0], (κ, γ), 0.0) @assert maximum(abs.(vec(sum(G; dims = 1)))) < 1e-12 @assert mass_error < 1e-8 ``` ::: Those two checks validate the *implementation*. They say nothing about the approximation itself, which is the substance of this chapter: the Gaussian increments of @eq-chemical-langevin replaced the exact Poisson reaction counts of the previous chapter, and only a comparison against that exact process can show what the replacement cost. A seed-by-seed path comparison is not meaningful here, because the two simulations do not share an explicitly coupled source of randomness: the same seed drives a Poisson event stream in one model and Gaussian increments on a fixed grid in the other. We therefore compare distributions, using the same reaction network as @sec-jump-processes as the reference. The epidemic peak is a good summary to compare because it depends on the whole trajectory. A longer horizon is used here than in the figure above, so that every path has peaked before the window closes. ::: {#cell-code-ch05-jump-comparison .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Catalyst using JumpProcesses using Statistics sir_network = @reaction_network begin κ, S + I --> 2I γ, I --> R end const comparison_tspan = (0.0, 60.0) function jump_peak(seed) problem = JumpProblem( sir_network, [:S => 990, :I => 10, :R => 0], comparison_tspan, [:κ => κ, :γ => γ]; aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(seed), ) return maximum(solve(problem, SSAStepper())[sir_network.I]) end function sde_peak(seed) problem = SDEProblem( sir_drift!, sir_diffusion!, u₀, comparison_tspan, (κ, γ); noise_rate_prototype = zeros(3, 2), ) solution = solve( problem, LambaEM(); dt = 0.02, adaptive = false, saveat = 0.1, rng = StableRNG(seed), ) return maximum(Array(solution)[2, :]) end M = 500 jump_peaks = [jump_peak(4000 + k) for k in 1:M] sde_peaks = [sde_peak(5000 + k) for k in 1:M] mean_difference = abs(mean(jump_peaks) - mean(sde_peaks)) mean_standard_error = sqrt((var(jump_peaks) + var(sde_peaks)) / M) spread_ratio = std(sde_peaks) / std(jump_peaks) @assert mean_difference < 3 * mean_standard_error (; jump_mean = round(mean(jump_peaks); digits = 1), sde_mean = round(mean(sde_peaks); digits = 1), mean_difference_in_standard_errors = round(mean_difference / mean_standard_error; digits = 2), jump_spread = round(std(jump_peaks); digits = 1), sde_spread = round(std(sde_peaks); digits = 1), spread_ratio = round(spread_ratio; digits = 2)) ``` ::: {#code-ch05-jump-comparison .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (jump_mean = 169.8, sde_mean = 169.8, mean_difference_in_standard_errors = 0.03, jump_spread = 23.3, sde_spread = 23.6, spread_ratio = 1.01) ``` ::: ::: The two mean peaks agree to well within the Monte Carlo error of the comparison, and the two standard deviations agree to a few percent. At $N=1000$ the diffusion therefore reproduces not just the location of the epidemic peak but how much it varies between outbreaks, which is the substantive claim the approximation makes and the reason it is worth using in place of an exact simulation. Note the scope of that claim: it concerns the mean and standard deviation of one summary, the peak. Agreement here supports the diffusion approximation for this summary in this regime; it does not establish that the two models have the same full trajectory distribution. Both numbers are estimates, so read them with the standard errors in mind rather than as exact agreement. The standard error above covers sampling uncertainty only. It says nothing about the SDE's time-discretization error, nor about the slight downward bias from reading the SDE peak off a `saveat = 0.1` grid, which can miss a maximum falling between saved points. The ensemble size matters too: with $M=40$ instead of 500 the ratio of standard deviations wanders between roughly 0.7 and 1.1 from one batch of seeds to the next, which would say more about the sample size than about the approximation. A comparison of variability needs more replicates than a comparison of means, because a standard deviation is itself estimated with a relative error of about $1/\sqrt{2M}$. This agreement is specific to the regime, not a general property, and the asymmetry between the two models is worth being clear about. Both models make the same modelling assumptions — this reaction network, mass-action propensities, homogeneous mixing, fixed parameters — and conditional on that CTMC the direct method adds nothing further: it introduces no time discretization and no diffusion approximation. It is the extra step to the diffusion that carries an approximation, because @eq-chemical-langevin needs each reaction to fire many times over an interval short enough that the propensities barely move. Those two requirements pull against each other, and both fail when a compartment is nearly empty. The tests in the exercises reduce $N$ and refine $\mathrm{d}t$, and at small populations the diffusion's failures are visible in exactly the quantities compared here. An ensemble comparison tests the approximation statistically; it does not make the diffusion exact. ## Interpretation and limitations The chemical Langevin equation is derived by replacing Poisson reaction counts with Gaussian increments. It is therefore fast and differentiable in much of the interior of the state space, but it can produce $S<0$, $I<0$, or $R<0$, especially near extinction, with large time steps, or in small populations. Clipping a trajectory after each step changes its probability law; it is a pragmatic visualization safeguard, not a principled boundary condition. Alternatives include the exact CTMC, nonnegative tau-leaping, reflecting/absorbing boundary schemes, or transforming the model. `noise_rate_prototype` is an API-level detail with mathematical meaning: leaving it out would ask for diagonal noise, not the two reaction noises in Equation @eq-chemical-langevin. The [StochasticDiffEq SDE tutorial](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/tutorials/sde_example/) documents `SDEProblem`, `EM`, and non-diagonal noise. The approximation itself is the chemical Langevin construction associated with reaction networks [@gillespie1977]. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch05-ex1} Run the SDE with `dt` values $0.1$, $0.05$, and $0.01$, using `adaptive=false` and a fixed seed for reproducibility. For each run, record the maximum conservation error and the minimum state value. Explain why conservation stays accurate to roundoff at every step size, whereas nonnegativity is not structurally preserved for a Gaussian diffusion. Do not read the differences between these runs as pathwise convergence. Using the same seed does not give the same Wiener path on different time grids: the solves draw random numbers at different times, so they realize different Brownian motions. A genuine pathwise convergence experiment needs the noise realization to be shared explicitly across the solves, which is what [`NoiseWrapper`](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqNoiseProcess/dev/abstract_noise_processes/) is for. ### Exercise 2 {#ch05-ex2} Construct a diagonal-noise SDE that keeps the same drift but adds independent noise to $S$, $I$, and $R$ with the same marginal instantaneous variances as the reaction-level model, that is $$ G_{\mathrm{diag}}=\operatorname{diag} \left(\sqrt{a_1},\ \sqrt{a_1+a_2},\ \sqrt{a_2}\right). $$ Compare its conservation error and infected trajectory with the reaction-level model. Identify the two off-diagonal covariance terms lost by this replacement, and show why the total-population increment now has nonzero variance. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/05-stochastic-differential-equations.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/05-stochastic-differential-equations.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/05-stochastic-differential-equations.jl)
